Last session we talked a bit about how you might scrape data from the web. Collecting data is not an end in itself, rather the first step in answering your research question. When it comes to analyzing trends, testing hypotheses, and predicting outcomes, modelling enters the picture.

In general, remember that your basic workflow for evaluating and reporting models is as follows:

![](pics/data-science-communicate.png)
Today we will mostly deal with the “Model” and “Communicate” steps shown in the graph.

To that end, we will cover:

- the basic intuition of how prediction models are set up and trained,
- how to train and evaluate a prediction model in `R`,
- how `tidymodels` can be used to make this process more efficient and robust,
- how to report models, using regression tables and plots.

:::{.alert-warning .pad-box}
This lab focuses on the "mechanics" of modelling. In practice, justifying which model to use (and interpreting the model) is arguably much more important than what we cover today. These aspects will be discussed at length in your future Machine Learning and Causal Inference courses, and in a lot of electives. Those of you who took Statistics II will already be familiar with some of these considerations.
:::
------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Setup

We again use the `flights` data from the [`nycflights13`](https://nycflights13.tidyverse.org/)
package, containing flights that departed from New York City in 2013.

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights13)
```

The full dataset contains more than 300,000 flights. To minimize the time our models run, we take a sample of 20,000 flights with a recorded arrival delay and retain a small set of possible predictors.

`slice_sample` samples randomly from the input dataframe. Whenever your code involves randomness, it is important to explicitly set a `seed` - the concrete value does not matter, just that it's constant. This will keep your code reproducible for you and your colleagues.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)

flights_dat <- nycflights13::flights |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(arr_delay)) |>
  dplyr::select(
    arr_delay, dep_delay, distance, origin, carrier
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    origin = factor(origin),
    carrier = factor(carrier)
  ) |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 20000)

dplyr::glimpse(flights_dat)
```

In general, we can use models in two different ways: 

- to test hypothesis, aka answering causal questions about our data
- to create predictions from the data, aka to learn the underlying data generating process.

Today, we will exclusively focus on the latter aspect of modeling, trying to **predict a flights arrival delay**.

:::{.alert-primary .pad-box}
All models we build during this lab are intended to be examples in order to get used to the workflow - we are not too concerned with building the best possible model or even models suitable for real-world use.
:::


# Modelling with usual R functions

First, we build the complete prediction pipeline with the tools that come with R and the `tidyverse` data-wrangling functions you already know. Once we build an intuition of the basic worklflow, we will see how we can make our lives easier using the packages bundled in `tidymodels`.

A prediction model learns a rule that maps a set of **predictors** to an
**outcome**. Here, the outcome is `arr_delay` - it is was we want to predict.
The predictors are what the model can use to predict the outcome.

Building a prediction model generally has two phases:

1. **Fitting** or **training** the model: Here, the model learns how to calculate the outcome based on the predictors. This usually means solving an optimization problem. For example, in OLS-regression, the model will calculate the set of regression coefficients that minimize the squared error. The prediction error is the difference between the value a model predicts and the true (known) outcome value.  

2. **Testing** or **evaluating** the model: Here, we present the trained model some data that it has not yet seen and again check how close our predictions are to the true outcome value. 

When building prediction models, we want to make sure that our model actually learned the *general idea* of the function connecting the predictors to the outcome. **We don't want our model to just memorize all the data** - instead, it should also give reasonable predictions when presented with data it has never seen before.

## 1. Split the data

We must evaluate predictions on observations that were not used to estimate the
model. We therefore randomly assign 80% of the flights to a training set and
reserve 20% as a test set. 80/20 is a common ratio between training and testing data.

```{r split}
# Get indices representing 80% of the data.
train_rows <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(flights_dat)),
  size = floor(0.80 * nrow(flights_dat))
)

# Lookup train and test set based on the indices
flights_train <- flights_dat |>
  dplyr::slice(train_rows)

flights_test <- flights_dat |>
  dplyr::slice(-train_rows)
```

From this point onward, the test set is not used train the model. It is only used to evaluate the finished prediction rule, aka the fitted model.

## 2. Specify and fit the model

Specifying a model involves writing down what relationship you expect between your outcome and your predictors. In R, we use **formulas** to specify these relationships.

The basic structure of a formula looks like this: `y ~ x`.

On the left side, we denote our outcome. On the right side come the predictors. In the simple case above, the formula says: Calculate `y` on basis of `x`. In OLS-regression, this calculation involves one regression coefficient for each predictor on the right side, and an intercept.

To fit a linear regression (OLS) model in R, we use the `lm` function. It takes the formula for our model and the data it should fit as parameters:

```{r usual-formula}
flight_formula <-
  arr_delay ~ dep_delay + distance + origin + carrier

lm_fit <- stats::lm(
  formula = flight_formula,
  data = flights_train # We fit the model only on the training data!
)

lm_fit
```

The fitted coefficients describe the prediction rule. For a new flight, R
multiplies each predictor by its fitted coefficient and adds the intercept.

For `carrier` and `origin`, our model has more than one coefficient - to be precise, it has one coefficient **for each individual value** that these columns have in our data. To utilize a **categorical** variable in a model, they need to be converted into numbers. R will take care of that for us, as we converted our categorical values into *factors* above.

## 3. Predict new observations

`predict()` applies the fitted rule to the predictors in `flights_test`. We keep
the observed arrival delay alongside each prediction so that we can calculate the
prediction errors: As already mentioned, that is the **difference between the true outcome and our prediction**.

```{r usual-predictions}
test_predictions <- flights_test |>
  dplyr::select(arr_delay) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    .pred = stats::predict(
      lm_fit, # Fitted Model
      newdata = flights_test # Attention: for predicting, use the test data!
    ),
    .error = arr_delay - .pred # Specify how to calculate prediction error
  )

dplyr::slice_head(test_predictions, n = 6)
```

The model nearly perfectly predicted some values! For others, it predicted values either too small or too large. Next, we will see how to systematically assess how good our model was, taking into account all of the data in our test set.

## 4. Evaluate the predictions

There are many different metrics on which you can evaluate how good a model is. Which ones to use depends on the precise task the model should solve. We will use three metrics which are very common for numerical prediction problems:

- **MAE**, the **mean absolute error**: Calculates the average distance between the prediction and the true value. Lower values are better.
- **RMSE**, the **root-mean-square-error**: Calculates the root of the average of the squared errors. It is more sensitive to outliers, as larger errors have a higher impact due to the squaring. Lower values are better.   
- **R-squared** describes how much of the variance in the true outcome value is captured by our model. Values are between 0 (the model captures no variance) and 1 (perfect, the model captures all variance).

```{r usual-metrics}
metrics <- tibble::tibble(
  .metric = c("mae", "rmse", "rsq"),
  .estimate = c(
    mean(abs(test_predictions$.error)),
    sqrt(mean(test_predictions$.error^2)),
    cor(
      test_predictions$arr_delay,
      test_predictions$.pred
    )^2
  )
)

metrics
```

Whether for example 12 for the MAE is high or not requires us to know the scale of the original data. If the maximum value of the outcome in the data is 5, an MAE of 12 would be quite bad. If most values would be in the thousands, 12 is a pretty small error. 

Let's take a look at a plot common to evaluate this, plotting our predictions against the true values:

```{r usual-prediction-plot, fig.height=4.5}
test_predictions |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = arr_delay, y = .pred)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = "#2f1a61") +
  ggplot2::coord_equal() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Observed arrival delay (minutes)",
    y = "Predicted arrival delay (minutes)",
    title = "Held-out predictions from the linear model"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

A perfect model would have all point directly on the diagonal - our model didn't do too bad! But we can also see that, especially for the flights with lower or no delays, the model was often off.

# The same model with `tidymodels`

Now we repeat the analysis using the **same training rows, test rows, formula,
and linear-regression engine**. This lets us see what `tidymodels` changes - and
what it does not change.

```{r}
library(tidymodels)
```

`tidymodels` is a collection of packages that apply tidyverse design principles
to modelling. **Recipes** can be used to describe preprocessing, `parsnip` provides a common model interface, and workflows keep preprocessing and the model together. The
[tidymodels cheat sheets](https://www.tidymodels.org/cheatsheets/) are useful
references after this session.

The tidymodels version follows four steps:

1. **Describe preprocessing** with a recipe.
2. **Specify** a model.
3. **Bundle** recipe and model in a workflow.
4. **Fit and evaluate** the workflow using the existing split.

## 1. Describe preprocessing with a recipe

A recipe records what should happen to the predictors. It is estimated using
training data and then applies the same learned transformations to new data - remember, we don't want any part of the modeling process to **see** any of the test data before the final prediction and evaluation.

```{r recipe}
flights_recipe <- recipes::recipe(
  flight_formula,
  data = flights_train
) |>
  recipes::step_dummy(recipes::all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  recipes::step_zv(recipes::all_predictors())

flights_recipe
```

Read the recipe from top to bottom. It:

- uses exactly the same formula as the first R model;
- creates indicator variables for categorical predictors such as `origin` and
  `carrier`; and
- removes predictors with no variation.

Once you specified your recipe, use `recipes::prep()` on `flights_recipe`, then use `recipes::bake()` with `new_data = NULL` to inspect the processed training data:

- What happened to `origin` and `carrier`?
- How many predictor columns does the prepared dataset contain?

```{r}
prepared_recipe <- recipes::prep(flights_recipe)
processed_train <- recipes::bake(prepared_recipe, new_data = NULL)

processed_train |>
  dplyr::glimpse()
```
Until now, you could argue that we did not gain much from using the recipe - we got the conversion for the categorical variables earlier for free as well, and we did not have any constant (zero variance) predictors in our data. However, there are many more preprocessing steps you might want to take for a more complex model, such as scaling or transforming variables. In these cases, using a recipe, and the many preprocessing functions the package provides is very useful to ensure you apply all the steps all the time and there is one canonical place for all of your preprocessing steps.

## 2. Specify a model, then create a workflow

`parsnip` provides a unified interface to **many different models**. This is nice because you only need to learn how to use `parsnip`, and not one new function per model - for example when comparing different prediction models for a specific prediction task for your thesis.

We again setup linear regression estimated with `lm()`:

```{r linear-workflow}
linear_spec <- parsnip::linear_reg() |>
  parsnip::set_engine("lm")

linear_workflow <- workflows::workflow() |>
  workflows::add_recipe(flights_recipe) |>
  workflows::add_model(linear_spec)

linear_workflow
```

The workflow keeps the recipe and model together. This makes it much harder to
forget a preprocessing step when fitting or predicting with new data. The `workflow` package also takes care of preparing and baking our preprocessing recipe for us - very kind.

```{r fit-linear}
tidymodels_fit <- linear_workflow |>
  parsnip::fit(data = flights_train)

tidymodels_fit |>
  workflows::extract_fit_parsnip()
```

`fit()` trains the model on the training data. To see how well the workflow
predicts new observations, we now apply it once to the held-out test data.

Compare the regression coefficient with the ones we got without `tidymodels` above - they are exactly the same! `tidymodels` makes the modeling workflow easier to scale, but the underlying concepts (and math!) stays exactly the same.

### Inspecting Models with `broom`

`broom` is another package from the `tidymodels` family that makes inspecting coefficients, etc. more pleasant - and again works for a wide variety of different models:

The `tidy` function gives you information about the different predictors in our fitted model. It returns a tibble, so it is easy to use the information returned by `tidy` for example to create a custom visualization.

```{r}
broom::tidy(tidymodels_fit)
```
The `glance` function gives you a single row of measures for how well our model fit the data - you can see R-squared there, that we already saw above. This is handy if you want to compare many different models. Again, you get the information in a tibble, so you can row-bind many of them.

```{r}
broom::glance(tidymodels_fit)
```

Finally, `augment` lets you see row-level informations for your predictions, such as the prediction error (redisual) for each prediction on your test data.

```{r}
broom::augment(tidymodels_fit, new_data = flights_test)
```

Under the hood, it of course needs to calculate the predictions to show you that information - let's take a look at how to predict ourselfes using `tidymodels` next!


## 3. Evaluate on the test set

`predict()` automatically applies the trained recipe before generating the
predictions. This is especially important if you have more complex preprocessing steps, as you need to ensure that, for example, the scales of variables stay the same in your train and test data.

We then combine the predictions with the observed outcomes and calculate three common regression metrics.

```{r test-predictions}
tidymodels_test_predictions <- predict(
  tidymodels_fit,
  new_data = flights_test
) |>
  dplyr::bind_cols(
    flights_test |>
      dplyr::select(arr_delay)
  )

tidymodels_metrics <- tidymodels_test_predictions |>
  yardstick::metrics(
    truth = arr_delay,
    estimate = .pred
  )

tidymodels_metrics
```

It should come as no surprise, that we get the same predictions, errors, and metrics as before - again, the model is exactly the same. We just took a different approach to building it.

```{r compare-approaches}
tibble::tibble(
  r = test_predictions$.pred,
  tidymodels = tidymodels_test_predictions$.pred
) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    largest_prediction_difference = max(abs(r - tidymodels))
  )

dplyr::bind_rows(
  "R" = metrics,
  "tidymodels" = tidymodels_metrics,
  .id = "approach"
)
```

The result is the same, but the recipe and model are now stored together in one
workflow. `predict()` applies the recipe automatically, and `yardstick` computes
the metrics with a consistent interface - and we didn't need to implement their math ourselves. 

Those advantages become more valuable as preprocessing and modelling pipelines grow.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Reporting model results

An important part of modeling is **communicating** your model to others.

Two of the most common ways to do that for regression models are regression tables and coefficient plots. Both can be easily generated using the `modelsummary` package.

## A regression table

```{r regression-table}
modelsummary::modelsummary(
  tidymodels_fit,
  estimate = "{estimate}",
  statistic = NULL,
  coef_omit = "Intercept",
  coef_rename = c(
    "dep_delay" = "Departure delay",
    "distance" = "Distance"
  ),
  gof_omit = "DF|Deviance|Log.Lik|AIC|BIC",
  title = "Linear models of arrival delay",
  notes = "Estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Training data from a sample of 20,000 NYC flights departing in 2013.",
  #output = "markdown"
)
```
As you can tell from the code above, `modelsummary` allows us to customize many different aspects of our regression table - for example, try to: 

- Include the intercept in the table above
- Change the output format of the table to markdown or LaTeX (very handy for your thesis!).

## A coefficient plot

Visualizations are usually a good way to making information easier to understand - and this is true for models as well! One common visualization is a coefficient plot, that we can also easily generate using `modelsummary` and `ggplot`: 

```{r coefficient-plot, fig.height=3.5}
modelsummary::modelplot(
  tidymodels_fit,
  coef_map = c("dep_delay" = "Departure delay")
) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Estimated coefficient (95% CI)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Association between departure and arrival delay"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

What does this tell us? The model uses a multiple of the departure delay when predicting the arrival delay - indicating that a plane usually gets a bit more delayed during travel, although not by much.

Coefficient plots become even more useful when you you include multiple predictors or even use them to compare multiple models. Let's try to include `distance` in our plot as well!

# Wrap-up

In theory, you do not need `tidymodels` to perform modeling in R - and as we have seen, the models do not care **how** they are fitted. However, the `tidymodels` collection of packages contains many packages that are especially useful when fitting more complex models including a lot of preprocessing (`recipes`), or running models on different data (`workflows`). 

Additionally, `broom` makes it easier to inspect properties of a fitted model and `yardstick` can help you calculate many different type of evaluation metrics, without worrying about implementing the math yourself.

For more complex models, `tidymodels` also includes packages for tuning hyperparameters and lots of other things...
